FACULTY SENATE OFFICE F ACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION January 23, 2025 Gr aduate Council Report #2024-2025-04 The following matter was discussed and recommended by the Graduate Council at their November, 2024 meeting after similar legislation was advanced in a joint action by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) and the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) last November. Their intent was to ensure a streamlined curricular approval process for online undergraduate courses, regardless of their calendar format The Graduate Council now requests that the Faculty Senate approve the same measure for graduate-level courses. Con text: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions). Pr oposed: Any course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms. Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-2 January 23, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.” Rationale: The “adopted” definitions are not memorialized in the University Manual and the current need to update modality-related descriptions provides an opportunity to provide standardized language in the University Manual, where it will be easily found and understood.
The language is proposed for insertion into Chapter 8, Academic Regulations (Regulations for Students), Section 30, Courses.

Existing modalities will translate into new modalities as follows: 1. ‘In-person’ � ‘In-person’ 2. ‘Blended’ � ‘In-person and online asynchronous’ or ‘In-person and online synchronous’ 3. ‘Online’ � ‘Online synchronous’ or ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’ or ‘Online asynchronous’.
Because current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses will need to be assigned to a new modality (perhaps more than one if multiple faculty teach the same course using different modalities), faculty/departments will be allowed to update the modality of current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses directly with the registrar without going through the standard course modification process.
A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities (‘In-person’, ‘In-person and online asynchronous’, ‘In-person and online synchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘in-person’ modalities.

A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘online’ modalities (‘Online synchronous’, ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’, ‘Online asynchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘online’ modalities.
As per current practice, course change proposals will continue to be necessary for courses with one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities that wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) one of the three ‘online’ modalities.
This is also true for ‘online’ modality courses that wish to adopt/add an ‘in-person’ modality.
Because of the volume of required changes, the new modalities will take effect starting in the Fall 2026 semester.

Existing Language: https://web.uri.edu/registration-records/faculty-staff-advisors/class-scheduling-process/ . “ In-person (I) : A course with no more than 24.9% of instruction delivered online.
All courses are assumed to be in-person unless otherwise approved by Faculty Senate.
Blended (B) : A course delivered 25%-74.9% online.
Online (O) : A course delivered at least 75% online.
Course must be approved as online by Faculty Senate to be scheduled as such.” Proposed Language: (To be inserted into Chapter 8 of the University Manual, “Academic Regulations.”) “ 8.30.30 Course Modality In-person : All instruction occurs in a specified physical location and on specified days/times.
In-person and online asynchronous : Instruction combines both in-person meetings on specified days/times and online asynchronous instruction.
The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class.

In-person and online synchronous : Instruction combines both in-person and online meetings on specified days/times. -person and online synchronous: Instruction combines both in-person and Online synchronous : All instruction occurs online at specified days/times.
Online synchronous and asynchronous : All instruction occurs online in a combination of synchronous meetings on specified days/times and asynchronous instruction.
The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus.
Online asynchronous : All instruction occurs online with no synchronous meetings required at specified days/times (outside of optional online office hours/meetings).
The weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction is clear to students in the syllabus.”

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

The competition among MSM programs is intense, with a large number of institutions offering these degrees.
Programs strive to differentiate themselves by emphasizing unique curricular components such as leadership development modules, capstone projects, or global immersion experiences, which are designed to enhance employability and prepare graduates for management roles.
The rise of digital learning technologies has also led many institutions to offer MSM programs in online or hybrid formats, further increasing their reach and intensifying competition as geographic barriers to enrollment are reduced.
To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATIONDECEMBER 12, 2024 Graduate CouncilReport 2024-2025-3B At the November 25, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate on December 12, 2024 for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM CHANGES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Student Personnel - MS Proposed changes include removal of “in College Student Personnel” in the degree title and reducing total credits required to 30 with 21 core courses.
Per the URI Grad school initiative to reduce total required credits for masters degrees, we have evaluated the CSP curriculum for duplicated content.
We also compared curricular content to national CAS standards to ensure that the program is in alignment with best practices.
The result is the removal of one class: EDC 529.
The course, in its entirety, no longer meets the needs of current CSP students.
The old curriculum map shows EDC 529 as only “R”einforcing Program Student Learning outcome #4.
And, that outcome is reinforced in two other courses and evaluated in EDC 580.
The program outcomes have not changed.

The existing outcomes can still be introduced, reinforced, and evaluated via the new changes.
Additionally, other CSP programs tend to have fewer credits than our current program.
The streamlining of our curriculum, particularly in regards to credit hours, aligns us with other programs nationally.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Environmental and Natural Resource Economics - PHD 3.
Reduce the number of credits required.
The graduate school now only requires 64 credits, so we are adjusting our program accordingly.
We are reducing credits to allow students to take advantage of the increased availability of ABD semesters. 4.
Allow for equivalent class to be taken in place of EEC502.
When teaching capacity is strained in our department, we have found several suitable replacements for this class, and we want them to be able to count when we are unable to offer EEC502. [A note to the reviewers: Our program description and admission requirements in Kuali did not reflect recent changes that had been approved.
We copied and pasted the current program description and admission

requirements into Kuali and then added items 2-4 above. 2-4 are the only changes we are requesting to the program description; all other changes have already been approved, as can be seen in the current catalog.] Proposed changes include removing “in Environmental and Natural Resource Economics” from the degree title and an initiation date of Spring 2025.
COLLEGE OF NURSING Nursing Practice - DNP Our current Program started as a BS to DNP Program and was put on hold about five years ago.
After that, we only accepted Post-Masters students for the in-person DNP Program.
Our current change to an Online Program will close both the Post BS to DNP and Post Masters to DNP in-person Programs.
Our current in-person DNP program attracts a small number of applicants each year.
Converting our program to an online, asynchronous, program offers expansion of the student pool from local to national.
There will be an overlap between teaching-out the in-person program and the start of the online offering.
We anticipate the last graduating class from the live program to be in the Spring Semester of 2027, while the first cohort to enter the online offering will be fall of 2025.

The proposed online program remains essentially the same with updates to some of the courses being delivered and a few new courses to enhance topical areas of integrative healthcare.
Teach-Out Plan: Students will be notified of the online plan and offered an LOA or postpone entry if they choose the online option.
Otherwise, the in-person DNP program will continue until students have completed which is anticipated to be Spring 2027.
To work in the URI online format, the 7-week sequence was required but the College wanted the extended time for each course for doctoral-level work (14 weeks), thus, the A/B model evolved for each course which is denoted with "A" 7 weeks plus "B" 7 weeks taken sequentially.
Attached is a sample of the course sequence for the NursingPractice-DNP Online.
Proposed program description: The Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) is an innovative, online, post master’s program that prepares advanced practice nurses as leaders in evidence based principles of traditional, complementary, and integrative health (TCIH) to transform health care systems.

Program Requirements: Program requirements include a minimum of 68 credits obtained as follows: 30 credits from a post MS degree and 38 credits to be completed to complete the DNP degree.
Program prerequisites include a master’s degree in nursing, completion of a 300- to 500-level statistics course, and a master’s level introduction research course.
DNP required NUR courses (32 credits) including NUR 662 (A&B), 664 (A&B), 672 (A&B), 673 (A&B), 674 (A&B), 675 (A&B), 676 (A&B), 677 (A&B) and 679 (A&B).
Also required are PHP XXX (A&B) and MBA XXX (A&B).
The program culminates with the clinical immersion practicum and a practice improvement project associated with NUR courses 677, 678, 679 (A&B sessions).
The Doctorate of Nursing Practice_DNP is a cohort model starting each fall and each cohort will complete the course sequence according to their program plan.

Proposed admission requirements: A master’s degree in nursing (GPA minimum 3.30); minimum R.N. licensure in the state student resides; completion of a 300- to 500-level statistics course; completion of a master’s level introduction to research course; completed application package with all transcripts; three letters of reference attesting to the applicant’s capability for doctoral study (academic and professional, at least one from a doctorally prepared nurse); one scholarly paper or a master’s thesis or equivalent; a statement of purpose indicating goals that are congruent with those of the program and institution and a curriculum vitae/resume.
Acceptance is based on a full review of the applicant’s record and not any single component.

NEW CERTIFICATES FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION College Teaching - Cert The 12 credit graduate certificate in college teaching is designed to prepare individuals to effectively teach in post-secondary settings–including college and community settings with adult learners. The graduate certificate will provide a knowledge base of adult learning theory and skills for instructional design, implementation and evaluation. It will also provide a solid foundation of teaching for equity and inclusion. COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES Community Planning - Cert (online) The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CPL), composed of 3 required classes and one elective, is an asynchronous online "stackable certificate" provides the pathway for working professionals to develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning. Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of site planning and environmental planning. Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement and professional growth. Class content in this certificate is geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge in planning. Completion of the certificate will provide a basic knowledge of planning that can be augmented with certificate programs in other departments, such as the Master of Public Administration (MPA), and the Master of Environmental Management (MEM) program.
